summary: Defines a MIME content type that a mail transfer agent or gateway can use to report the outcome of trying to deliver a message to one or more recipients. It was replaced by RFC 3464.

eli5.summary: This describes the form a post office fills out to tell you what happened to your letter, in a layout that mail programs can read automatically.

subtitle: A machine-readable MIME format for the reports mail systems send back about whether a message was delivered.

tldr.problem: Delivery failure and success reports in Internet mail came in many ad hoc, human-oriented forms, which made them hard for programs to process and hard to carry across gateways to other mail systems.
tldr.mechanism: A delivery status notification is a MIME multipart/report message whose second part, message/delivery-status, holds RFC 822 style fields: per-message fields, then one group of per-recipient fields with an action and a status code.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1894 has been obsoleted by RFC 3464, which is the definition to use today.

today: RFC 1894 was obsoleted by RFC 3464, and was updated by RFC 2852 before that. Its status is listed as Proposed Standard, but the replacement is the current definition.

sections.title: What a Delivery Status Notification Is
sections.content:
This memo defines a MIME content-type, message/delivery-status, for delivery status notifications (DSNs). A DSN tells the sender of a message about failed delivery, delayed delivery, successful delivery, or the gatewaying of the message into an environment that may not support DSNs. It is meant to be used inside the multipart/report content type defined in RFC 1892, and it is a machine-processable replacement for the various notifications then in use in Internet mail.

Only the format is defined here. An extension to SMTP that fully supports requesting such notifications is left to a separate memo, RFC 1891. Because many messages cross between the Internet and other systems such as X.400, the format can carry "foreign" addresses and error codes, and extra attributes can be defined to tunnel foreign notifications through Internet mail.

Its stated purposes include telling people the status of delivery largely independent of human language, letting user agents track sent messages, letting mailing list exploders maintain subscriber lists automatically when deliveries repeatedly fail, and giving remote MTA maintainers enough information to understand reported errors.
sections.eli5: It is a standard form for the 'we could not deliver your letter' note, so that both people and mail programs know where to find each fact.

sections.title: The Four MTAs in a Report
sections.content:
A message may pass through several message transfer agents (MTAs), and each may see a different, rewritten recipient address. The RFC therefore names four roles:

  • Original MTA: the one the sender submits the message to.
  • Received-From MTA: the one the Reporting MTA received the message from and accepted responsibility for.
  • Reporting MTA: the one reporting the results of delivery attempts in the DSN.
  • Remote MTA: the next hop that could not accept the message, or refused responsibility for it.

Because addresses and status codes differ between mail systems, the fields that carry them have a type subfield, such as the rfc822 address-type, the smtp diagnostic-type or the dns MTA-name-type, followed by plain text in that format. IANA maintains a registry of these types, and names beginning with X- are reserved for experimental use.
sections.eli5: A letter may pass through several post offices. The report names which one first took the letter, which one is writing the note, and which one refused it.

sections.title: Shape of a DSN Message
sections.content:
A DSN is a MIME message with the top-level type multipart/report and the report-type parameter delivery-status. It has up to three components: first a human-readable explanation, second the message/delivery-status part, and third, optionally, the original message or part of it.

The DSN MUST be addressed, in both header and envelope, to the return address in the envelope of the original message, which for SMTP is the MAIL FROM address. When SMTP carries a DSN, the MAIL FROM command MUST use a NULL return address, MAIL FROM:<>, so DSNs do not generate mail loops. The From header SHOULD hold the address of a human responsible for the mail system, such as Postmaster.

One DSN describes exactly one message, but may cover several recipients, and several DSNs may be issued for one submission. The message/delivery-status body uses RFC 822 header field syntax, in 7bit encoding. Per-message fields come first, then a blank line, then one or more groups of per-recipient fields, each group preceded by a blank line.
sections.eli5: The note has three parts: a friendly explanation for people, a neat form for computers, and, if useful, a copy of the original letter.

sections.title: Per-Message and Per-Recipient Fields
sections.content:
The per-message fields appear at most once. Reporting-MTA is required. Optional ones are Original-Envelope-Id (which identifies the submission transaction and is not the same as the Message-Id), DSN-Gateway (which MUST appear if a gateway translated a foreign notification, and MUST NOT otherwise), Received-From-MTA and Arrival-Date.

Each group of per-recipient fields requires Final-Recipient, Action and Status. Optional fields are Original-Recipient, Remote-MTA, Diagnostic-Code, Last-Attempt-Date and Will-Retry-Until, which is allowed only for delayed DSNs.

The Status field is a transport-independent code in three numeric subfields separated by dots. The first subfield says whether the attempt succeeded (2 success, 4 persistent temporary failure, 5 permanent failure), the second gives the probable source of the problem, and the third a precise condition. The action and status can look redundant but are not: a temporary failure code can go with either delayed or failed, for example when retries finally stop. Diagnostic-Code keeps the transport's own code. Extension fields not starting with X- must be registered with IANA and published in an RFC.
sections.eli5: The form has boxes for who the letter was for, what happened to it, and a number code that says whether it worked, might work later, or never will.

sections.title: Conformance, Gateways and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
A minimal implementation need generate only Reporting-MTA per message, and Final-Recipient, Action and Status per recipient, although other fields are strongly recommended. An MTA MUST NOT generate Original-Recipient unless the transport provides the address the sender originally gave. Each sender-specified recipient SHOULD produce at most one delivered or failed DSN.

The appendices give non-binding guidance for gateways. When translating a foreign notification into a DSN, the gateway should supply reasonable values for the required fields, fall back on generic codes such as 2.0.0, 4.0.0 and 5.0.0 when needed, keep the foreign code in Diagnostic-Code, and name itself in DSN-Gateway. Going the other way, it should use the closest available approximation and preserve the original recipient and envelope identifier where it can.

For mailing lists, because DSNs go to the envelope return address, the list maintainer receives all of them and can process them mechanically to delete invalid subscribers.
sections.eli5: Even a very short note must say which post office wrote it, who it was for, what happened and the result code. Fancier notes can add more.

sections.title: Forgery, Confidentiality and Reliability
sections.content:
DSNs may be forged as easily as ordinary Internet mail. Threats include a falsified delivery or non-delivery notification, a falsified Final-Recipient or Remote-MTA, a falsified relay notification, and unsolicited DSNs. Programs that use DSNs automatically should take precautions against denial-of-service attacks.

Confidentiality is another concern: someone who auto-forwards mail may not want to reveal the forwarding address. The RFC lists ways to protect it, such as issuing a relayed or delivered DSN, omitting Remote-* or extension fields, using the NULL reverse-path, or disabling notifications with NOTIFY=NEVER. It warns that many existing MTAs wrongly send non-delivery notices to the header return address rather than the envelope address, which can defeat such protection.

Finally, a failed DSN cannot be relied on as proof that a message was not received. A race in SMTP can duplicate a message when a connection drops after the DATA command completes, so one copy may arrive while another is reported as failed.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake 'could not deliver' note, and a note saying 'failed' does not always mean the letter did not arrive. So take such notes with a grain of salt.

items.label: Failed
items.desc: Could not be delivered; the MTA has stopped trying and no further notice is expected.

items.label: Delayed
items.desc: Not delivered yet, but the MTA will keep trying; more notices may follow.

items.label: Delivered
items.desc: Delivered to the sender's chosen address (not necessarily read). A terminal state.

items.label: Relayed
items.desc: Passed into an environment that does not generate DSNs on delivery.

items.label: Expanded
items.desc: Delivered and forwarded on to multiple addresses; not a terminal state.

Reporting-MTA: dns; mta.example.org

Final-Recipient: rfc822; user@example.net
Action: failed
Status: 5.0.0
Diagnostic-Code: smtp; 550 mailbox unavailable
